level-1.title: Money that grows
summary: When you keep money in a bank, the bank pays you extra money.
This extra money is called interest.
The bank pays you because it can use your money for a while.
The longer you leave it, the more interest you get.
Money in a piggy bank does not grow. Money in a bank does.

questions.prompt: Why does a bank pay you interest just for keeping your money there?

image.alt: A small plant growing from a coin inside a bank

options.label: Because the bank gets to use your money while it is there, and pays you for that
Because banks enjoy giving away money
Because the government orders them to give gifts

questions.hint: Recall what the bank actually does with money while you are not using it.

questions.prompt: You have ₹200. Keeping it in a piggy bank for a year, or in a bank account for a year — in which case would you have MORE than ₹200 after that year, and why?

image.alt: A piggy bank next to a bank building, both holding two hundred rupees

options.label: The bank account — only it pays interest on top of what you put in
The piggy bank — it is safer so it grows more
Both would have exactly ₹200

questions.hint: Only one of the two options ever adds anything extra.

questions.prompt: You could save toward a goal that needs the money back in 1 month, or a goal in 12 months, both using a bank account. In which case will interest matter more to your final total, and why?

image.alt: A calendar showing one month and twelve months side by side

options.label: The 12-month goal — interest needs time to add up meaningfully
The 1-month goal — interest is always the same regardless of time
Neither — interest only applies to goals over ₹1000

questions.hint: Interest is small over a short time and adds up over a long time.

level-2.title: How interest is worked out
summary: The interest rate is written as a percent for one year.
5 percent means the bank adds ₹5 for every ₹100 you keep.
If you keep ₹1000 at 5 percent, after one year you have ₹1050.
Interest also works the other way. If you borrow, you pay interest.
A higher rate is good when you save. A higher rate is bad when you borrow.

questions.prompt: You keep ₹2000 in an account at 5 percent interest for one year. How much will you have at the end?

image.alt: A bar growing slightly taller, labelled two thousand rupees

questions.hint: 5 percent of 2000 is 100. Add that to the original amount.

questions.prompt: Two rates are on offer: 3% and 9%. Person A is saving money in an account. Person B is borrowing money for a loan. Which rate should each person prefer, and why?

image.alt: A saver and a borrower each facing two different interest rates

options.label: A should prefer 9% (more earned); B should prefer 3% (less owed)
Both should prefer 9%, since higher is always better
Both should prefer 3%, since lower is always safer

questions.hint: A higher rate benefits whoever is receiving interest, and costs whoever is paying it.

questions.prompt: You put ₹800 into an account. After a year at 5 percent interest, you have ₹840. What is the ₹800 called, and what is the ₹40?

image.alt: A starting stack of coins beside a smaller added stack

options.label: ₹800 is the principal; ₹40 is the interest earned
₹800 is the interest; ₹40 is the principal
Both amounts are called principal

questions.hint: The principal is what you started with, before anything was added.

level-3.title: Compound interest and time
summary: Simple interest is paid only on the money you first put in.
Compound interest is paid on your money and on the interest already earned.
₹10,000 at 8 percent compound becomes about ₹21,600 after ten years.
Starting early matters more than starting with a large amount.
Credit cards charge compound interest too. Unpaid balances grow quickly.

questions.prompt: ₹1000 grows at 10 percent a year. After year one it is ₹1100. If the interest is COMPOUND, what happens in year two?

image.alt: A curve rising faster over two years

options.label: You earn 10% of ₹1100, not just of the original ₹1000
You earn 10% of ₹1000 again, exactly the same as year one
No further interest is earned after year one

questions.hint: Compound interest is paid on the new, larger total — not the original amount.

questions.prompt: Person A saves ₹500 a month starting at age 15. Person B saves ₹1000 a month but starts at age 25, and both stop at 35. Whose final amount benefits more from compounding, and why might it be closer than expected?

image.alt: Two timelines, one ten years longer than the other

options.label: Person A — the extra 10 years lets compounding work for far longer, even saving less each month
Person B — saving twice as much each month always wins
They will always end with exactly the same amount

questions.hint: Compounding needs TIME above almost everything else, as the lesson stresses.

questions.prompt: You owe ₹5000 on a credit card at a high compound rate and pay nothing for two billing cycles in a row. What happens to the amount you owe between the first and second cycle?

image.alt: A card bill with a rising amount across two cycles

options.label: It grows faster in the second cycle, because interest is now charged on the first cycle's interest too
It grows by the same fixed amount each cycle
It stops growing after the first cycle

questions.hint: Just like savings, compound interest builds on the previous total — but here that total is a debt.
